# Inclusion & exclusion

::: {.question}
**What kind of criteria are you applying?**

- [Keep only participants who meet inclusion criteria](10-filter.qmd#sec-filter-keep)
- [Drop participants who meet exclusion criteria](10-filter.qmd#sec-filter-out)
- [Both — apply a full inclusion/exclusion checklist](10-filter.qmd#sec-filter-both)
:::

## Filter rows to keep — inclusion criteria {#sec-filter-keep}

::: {.pkgs}
Packages: `dplyr`
:::

Use filter() when you can describe who you want to KEEP. Watch out: filter() treats NA like FALSE, so rows with a missing value on your filtering variable get silently dropped too — not just the rows that truly fail the criteria.

```r
library(dplyr)

# keep only participants who consented and are 18+
survey_raw <- survey_raw |>
  filter(consent == "Yes", age >= 18)
```

::: {.callout-tip}
Because filter() drops NA rows on the condition, always compare `nrow()` before and after, and check whether anyone was dropped only because of a missing value rather than truly failing the criteria.
:::

::: {.next-steps}
**Where to next:**

:::

## Filter rows out — exclusion criteria {#sec-filter-out}

::: {.pkgs}
Packages: `dplyr`
:::

filter_out(), added in dplyr 1.2.0, is the companion to filter() built specifically for describing who you want to REMOVE. Unlike a negated filter() (using !condition), filter_out() treats NA like FALSE too — so participants with a missing value on your exclusion variable are correctly kept rather than accidentally dropped. Requires dplyr 1.2.0 or later (`packageVersion("dplyr")` to check).

```r
library(dplyr)

# drop anyone who withdrew consent, or failed the attention check
survey_raw <- survey_raw |>
  filter_out(consent == "Withdrew", attention_check == "Failed")

# compare: the old, error-prone way to write the same thing with filter()
# survey_raw |> filter(!(consent == "Withdrew" & attention_check == "Failed"))
# ...that version silently mishandles any row with an NA in either column
```

::: {.callout-tip}
Reach for filter_out() any time you catch yourself writing `!=` or wrapping a condition in `!( )` to describe who to exclude — that's exactly the pattern it replaces.
:::

:::

## Apply a full inclusion/exclusion checklist {#sec-filter-both}

::: {.pkgs}
Packages: `dplyr`
:::

Most studies apply both at once — keep the eligible, then drop the excluded. Doing this as two explicit steps (rather than one long condition) keeps your criteria easy to read back later, e.g. when writing a participant-flow paragraph for a methods section.

```r
library(dplyr)

n_start <- nrow(survey_raw)

survey_raw <- survey_raw |>
  # inclusion: keep only eligible participants
  filter(consent == "Yes", age >= 18) |>
  # exclusion: drop anyone who should be removed even if eligible
  filter_out(attention_check == "Failed", duplicate_flag == TRUE)

n_end <- nrow(survey_raw)
n_start - n_end   # how many participants were removed
```

::: {.callout-tip}
Keep a running count like `n_start`/`n_end` for every inclusion/exclusion step — it's exactly the number you'll need for a CONSORT-style participant flow description.
:::
